newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: NATO-Russia pact gives boost to arms cuts talks.
newsitem.headline: NATO-Russia pact gives boost to arms cuts talks.

text.p: A NATO-Russia accord on a new post-Cold War security relationship has given a boost to talks in Vienna on modernising a key treaty on conventional arms cuts, diplomatic sources said on Friday.

Thirty signatory states of the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, including the United States and Russia, agreed at a summit in Lisbon in December to restructure the pact to reflect the new face of Europe after the collapse of the Warsaw Pact and breakup of the Soviet Union.
"There is a noticeable shift in the energy and propulsion of the negotiating process as a result of the NATO-Russia agreement," a Western diplomatic source close to the Vienna talks said.

Ratification by the 30 states of changes to flank limitations -- the numbers of weaponry and troops the CFE allows nations to station on its borders -- has also spurred on negotiations, the source said.
All ratification documents by the 30 were deposited by the deadline on May 15.

Moscow had been pushing for more than five years to alter military quotas on its borders after its frontiers changed in 1991 with the demise of the Soviet Union and the birth of new independent republics, such as Ukraine and the Baltic states.

All 16 members of the NATO military alliance recognised the CFE had to be adapted to answer Russia's concerns over flashpoints in its border areas, in particular after its experience in Chechnya, and the potential for further trouble in the Caucasus region.
Diplomatic sources say a willingness by the West to accommodate Russia's concerns on arms quotas may have gone some way to assuage its fears of NATO's eastward expansion.
"It seems that Russia is now capable of living with an expanded NATO," one envoy said.
The Russian government would also be able to sell the idea of a bigger NATO more easily back home if it can show it had new flexibility in meeting any security threat on its frontiers.

The CFE pact was negotiated during the Cold War divide with quotas of military equipment balanced between the two rival blocs. More than 50,000 pieces of armour were destroyed by a 1995 deadline, including 19,000 battle tanks, 18,000 armoured vehicles, and thousands of artillery weapons, combat aircraft and attack helicopters.

The current Vienna talks, launched after an Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) summit last December, now aims to change to the "two-bloc" quota system for another. Russia had argued that the disappearance of the communist bloc had tipped the CFE pact out of kilter in favour of NATO.
"This is intended to be a successor to the 1990 treaty...but in no way will the ceilings (of weapons and troops) be higher than they were before," another diplomatic source said.

NATO has been pushing for national arms ceilings, to which Moscow reacted coolly. But soundings among delegations suggest a compromise may be found whereby national ceilings would be coupled with "territorial ceilings", the source said.
So, for example, one territory may include "central Europe", totalling quotas for Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, while another territory may include the Balkan nations.
The concept of territorial ceilings is still on the drawing board but Western envoys are optimistic that the new treaty could be ready by early next year or even the end of 1997.
